oneLineAnswer: A prescription tablet that raises a low platelet count before a procedure or in immune thrombocytopenia.
whatItIs: Avatrombopag is a prescription-only medicine sold in the United States under the brand name DOPTELET. It comes as 20 mg film-coated tablets and as 10 mg granules inside a capsule. The granule form is made for young children. It belongs to a drug group called thrombopoietin receptor agonists. Thrombopoietin is your body's own chemical signal for making platelets. Avatrombopag imitates that signal. The US regulator first approved it in 2018. It is a small synthetic molecule, not a biologic or a blood product.
whatItDoes: It tells bone marrow cells called megakaryocytes to multiply and mature, so your body makes more platelets.
In the label's studies, platelet counts began rising in 3 to 5 days and peaked at 10 to 13 days.
It is approved for adults with chronic liver disease who are scheduled for a procedure.
It is also approved for adults and children with immune thrombocytopenia who responded poorly to earlier treatment.
The label describes adjusting how much and how often to hold platelet counts above the prescriber's target.
howPeopleUseIt: This is a specialist medicine, given by a doctor, not something you buy on your own.
The label says to take it with food.
For chronic liver disease, treatment is short: a few days before the planned procedure.
For immune thrombocytopenia, treatment usually continues, and blood tests guide any change.
Tablets and granules are not interchangeable at the same milligram amount.
The granules are mixed into soft food or liquid and taken right away.
In the United States only one brand exists, DOPTELET.
There is no supplement or over-the-counter version.

commonSideEffects: In chronic liver disease trials, the most frequent problems were fever, belly pain, nausea, headache, tiredness, and leg swelling.
In adult immune thrombocytopenia, headache and tiredness were common.
So were bruising, nosebleeds, upper respiratory infection, joint pain, and gum bleeding.
Tiny red skin spots and cold-like symptoms also occurred.
In children with immune thrombocytopenia, common problems were viral infection, cold-like symptoms, cough, fever, and sore throat.
seriousSigns: Blood clots are the main serious concern.
The label warns that this drug class has been linked to clots in arteries and veins.
Among adults treated for immune thrombocytopenia, arterial or venous clots occurred in 9 of 128 people, or 7%.
Among people with chronic liver disease, a portal vein clot occurred in 1 of 274, or 0.4%.
The label warns against giving it only to bring platelet counts back to normal.
Taking too much can push platelet counts too high and raise clot risk.
The label states that no antidote is known.
whoShouldAvoid: The label lists no absolute contraindication, so no group is barred outright.
The label says it may harm a fetus, based on animal studies.
Human pregnancy data are too thin to measure the risk.
Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for two weeks after the last dose.
People with known clot risk factors, such as Factor V Leiden, need that added risk weighed.
Children younger than 1 year fall outside the labeled age range.
Use in that group has not been established.

interactions: Medicines that strongly block the liver enzymes CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 can raise avatrombopag levels in your body.
Medicines that strongly speed up those same two enzymes can lower avatrombopag levels and may weaken it.
For persistent or chronic immune thrombocytopenia, the label recommends changing the dose when either type is used together.
For chronic liver disease, the label recommends no dose change with these medicines.
Avatrombopag is broken down mainly by CYP2C9 and CYP3A4.
Anything affecting those enzymes can change how long it stays active.
pregnancyAndChildren: In animal studies, avatrombopag harmed developing offspring in rabbits and rats. Those animals received exposures higher than patients do. Human pregnancy data are too limited to measure the risk of birth defects or miscarriage. The label states it may cause fetal harm. Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for two weeks after the last dose. Nobody knows whether the drug passes into human milk. It was found in the milk of rats. For children, the tablet is approved from age 6 and the granules from age 1. Both are for persistent or chronic immune thrombocytopenia after a poor response to earlier treatment. The label does not establish use in children younger than 1 year.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Nobody knows whether avatrombopag gets into human breast milk.
How it might affect a breastfed baby is unknown.
How it might affect milk supply is unknown.
Human pregnancy data are too thin to measure the risk of birth defects or miscarriage.
The label says the effect of severe kidney impairment is unknown, including in people on dialysis.
Clinical studies did not include enough people aged 65 and older to show a difference.
A trial for low platelets in people with cancer and liver disease was withdrawn because too few people joined.
Long-term effects in children are not well described.
Young rats given high doses for ten weeks developed changes in the stomach lining.
The fetched sources do not show whether raising platelet counts changes bleeding events or survival.
